subject: physics
title: Required practical: resistance and I–V characteristics
key_idea: Resistance is found by measuring the current in a component and the potential difference across it, then using R = V ÷ I. The same circuit tests how resistance changes with the length of a wire, and gives I–V graphs for different components.

sections.heading: Investigating the resistance of a wire

blocks.text: This practical finds how the resistance of a wire depends on its length, at constant temperature.

items: Equipment: power supply, ammeter, voltmeter, variable resistor, the wire fixed to a ruler, and crocodile clips.
The ammeter is in series with the wire. The voltmeter is in parallel with the wire.
The **independent variable** is the length of wire. The **dependent variable** is its resistance.
Result: resistance increases as the length of wire increases. Doubling the length approximately doubles the resistance, so the graph is a straight line through the origin.

diagram.alt: Put the steps of the wire-length investigation in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the method in the right order.
steps: Set up the circuit with the ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the wire.
Measure the length of wire between the crocodile clips with a ruler.
Close the switch and record the current and the potential difference.
Move a crocodile clip to change the length and repeat the readings.
Repeat each length, calculate mean values and remove anomalous readings.
Calculate the resistance for each length using R = V ÷ I.
Plot a graph of resistance against length.

diagram.alt: Calculate the resistance of a wire from a voltmeter and ammeter reading.
diagram.question: The voltmeter reads {V} V and the ammeter reads {I} A for a length of wire. Calculate the resistance of the wire.

blocks.text: Keeping the test fair and safe

items: Use the variable resistor to keep the current the same, so the temperature of the wire stays constant.
Keep the current low and disconnect the circuit between readings, to minimise heating of the wire.
The hazard is a high current. It may make the wire overheat or melt, and may cause burns. Use low currents.
Repeat the readings, calculate means and remove anomalous readings.
Measure current with an ammeter and potential difference with a voltmeter, then calculate R = V ÷ I.
Change only the length of the wire.
Keep the temperature constant by using a low current and the variable resistor.

blocks.text: The same meters give the I–V graph of a component such as a filament lamp, a diode or a resistor.

items: Put an ammeter in series with the component and a voltmeter in parallel with it.
Use a variable resistor, a variable power pack or a different number of cells to change the current and the potential difference.
The variable resistor changes the current in the circuit.
Reverse the connections to the power supply to obtain negative values.
Plot current against potential difference.
To test a fixed resistor instead of a lamp, swap the component and measure the current for different potential differences.
A variable resistor in series with the lamp gives a continuously variable potential difference.
A data logger collects many pairs of readings in a short time and measures current and potential difference at the same time.
Vary the potential difference, record current and potential difference, and plot an I–V graph.
Reverse the connections to get negative values.
A variable resistor changes the current in the circuit.

checks.q: In the wire-length investigation, which two meters are used and how is each connected?
checks.a: An ammeter in series with the wire and a voltmeter in parallel with the wire.

checks.q: Explain why the variable resistor is adjusted each time the length of wire is changed.
checks.a: It changes the resistance of the circuit to keep the current the same, so the temperature of the wire stays constant.

checks.q: Describe how to obtain negative values of potential difference when plotting an I–V graph.
checks.a: Reverse the connections to the power supply (or battery).

worked_example.question:
A student investigated how the resistance of a piece of wire varies with its length. The circuit included a variable resistor.

Explain why the student needed to adjust the variable resistor each time she changed the length of the wire.
answer_points: The variable resistor changes the resistance of the circuit.
To keep the current the same.
So the temperature of the wire is kept constant.
worked_example.tip: Three linked steps: resistance of the circuit, current kept the same, temperature of the wire constant.

worked_example.question:
Students determine the resistance of a piece of iron wire. Their circuit has a power supply, an ammeter, a voltmeter and a variable resistor.

The variable resistor is used to prevent the iron wire from becoming too hot.

Explain how the variable resistor is used to prevent the iron wire from becoming too hot.
answer_points: The variable resistor increases the resistance of the circuit.
So the current is kept constant (or smaller).
Because the current heats up the wire (this can replace one of the other points).
worked_example.tip: Any two linked points score. Adjusting the variable resistor to keep the current constant or small gets both marks.

worked_example.question:
A student sets up a circuit to investigate the resistance of a lamp. The circuit has an ammeter and a voltmeter.

Explain how you could use the same circuit to investigate the resistance of a fixed resistor instead of a lamp.
answer_points: Change the lamp for a (fixed) resistor.
Measure the current for different potential differences.
worked_example.tip: Repeating the experiment is also allowed for the second mark.
